lesson.title: No Two Samples Alike: Understanding Sampling Variability
lesson.summary: Different random samples from the same population almost never produce identical statistics, and that scatter, called sampling variability, is a built-in feature of random sampling, not a mistake.
lesson.body:
A sample is just one particular subset of a population, and a statistic, like a sample proportion or sample mean, is a number computed from that one subset. Because different random samples pick up different individuals, even from the exact same population using the exact same sampling method, the resulting statistic will typically come out a little different each time. This scatter in the value of a statistic from sample to sample is called sampling variability, and it is not an error to be fixed, it's an unavoidable consequence of the fact that a sample is not the whole population.

Suppose, purely for illustration, that exactly 60% of students at a large school favor a proposed change to the lunch schedule, so the true population proportion is p = 0.6 (in practice this true value is essentially always unknown, which is the whole reason sampling gets used, but assuming it here makes the point easier to see). Now take four separate random samples of n = 10 students each and ask each student their opinion. Sample 1 might come back with 7 out of 10 in favor, a sample proportion of phat = 0.70. Sample 2 might come back with 5 out of 10, phat = 0.50. Sample 3 might land on 6 out of 10, phat = 0.60. Sample 4 might come back with 8 out of 10, phat = 0.80.

None of these four samples is wrong, and none of them is more correct than the others just because it happens to land closer to the true 0.6. Each is a legitimate outcome of randomly selecting 10 students from a population where the true rate is 60%, and which particular 10 students get picked, purely by chance, is enough to swing the sample proportion up or down. This is different from bias, which refers to a sampling method that systematically tends to miss the true value in some direction. Sampling variability is present even with a perfectly fair, unbiased sampling method, simply because a sample of 10 cannot perfectly mirror a population of thousands every single time.

If you could somehow repeat this same sampling process not four times but every possible time, listing the sample proportion from every single possible sample of 10 students, that full collection of outcomes would itself form a distribution. That distribution is the subject of the next chapter.
